To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
coronary blood flow and myocardial oxygen uptake are normal at rest and during exercise in subjects with severe aortic valve disease.

the myocardium of the patient with severe aortic valve disease is not only hypoxic but also has a reduced coronary flow reserve, which is the ability of the coronary vessels to increase their flow in response to an increased demand.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods and techniques to improve the understanding and diagnosis of heart disease.
the study of the effects of aortic valvular heart disease on the human coronary circulation and myocardial metabolism during exercise.
the development of new methods for the detection and treatment of coronary artery disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
coronary blood flow is normal in subjects with a stenotic aortic valve at rest and during exercise.
coronary flow is normal or even increased in patients with aortic valve lesions and that the myocardium has a high capacity for aerobic metabolism.
coronary flow is not significantly altered in severe aortic valve disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the coronary blood flow in the presence of severe aortic valve disease is not only adequate for the metabolic needs of the myocardium but is capable of further increase during exercise.
the coronary flow reserve is reduced, but the myocardium is able to extract the oxygen from the blood to maintain the oxygen consumption.

the coronary circulation of patients with severe aortic valve disease, in whom myocardial function is severely impaired, adapts to the situation and maintains a coronary flow that appears to be appropriate to the metabolic needs of the myocardium.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we can now measure blood flow in real time, and we can do it in the human brain, and we can measure it in the human heart, and we can see how the blood flows in the heart and brain during exercise and during sleep.
the heart is a very adaptable organ.
the brain is not the only organ that is affected by a lack of oxygen during exercise, and that the heart may be a target for this effect as well.
